Insights for realistically parameterizing a modeling construct of customer WTP is especially challenging in the absence of relevant data, a common occurrence when the policy of interest is novel, untested, and/or has no implementation precedent in the context of the research question. To address this challenge, we present as a case study a notional industry-wide carbon tax that is implemented in an agent-based model of the ATS. publications.title: The Polls---Trends: Support for Government Provision of Health Care and the ACA
publications.description: Since the 1930s, US politicians have argued whether healthcare should be the responsibility of the federal government. Both major political parties have cited public opinion concerning Americans’ support for/rejection of government provision of healthcare to support their position. With the passage of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act (ACA) in 2010, the political debate changed – where it had been about the government provision of healthcare as an abstract principle, it became a debate tinged with evaluations of the implementation of the ACA. This spawned a new line of research examining the consequences of the ACA’s implementation on public attitudes towards government provision of healthcare. The change in what support for government provision of health care questions measure and the new post-ACA research highlight a gap in the literature – a long-term examination of trends in support over the past two decades that will provide context for the new studies. This study aims to close that gap.

publications.title: The Polls—Trends: Support for Defense and Military Spending
publications.description: Recent political debates over solutions to the federal budget deficit and the ending of the past decade’s wars in Afghanistan and Iraq have likely put defense and military spending on the chopping block. Does the American public support such a policy choice? Are Americans more or less supportive of defense and military spending than they were prior to September 11, 2001?  This article reviews academic, independent, and media polls to address these questions. We find that levels of support for defense and military spending remain above “normal levels” between 1960 and 2000. We also find that although Americans are still opposed to cutting defense and military spending, they are more likely to support such cuts as a solution to the federal budget deficit after 2007.

publications.title: Aligning Wildfire Management Resourcing Decisions With Operational Needs
publications.description: A hierarchical modeling and simulation (M&S) framework can help federal agencies integrate the myriad business resourcing decisions they face as unmanned aerospace vehicle (UAV) systems are deployed within their federally authorized charters. An integrated M&S method offers a pragmatic approach to leveraging the power of analytical techniques and coping with the complex support requirements of modern macrosystems. In this paper, we demonstrate the benefits of incorporating several agent-based modeling (ABM) enhancements for UAV route planning into a hierarchical M&S structure.

publications.title: Framing Peace Policies: The Competition for Resonant Themes
publications.description:
Political organizations make use of culturally resonant symbols to bring their message
to the public. In response to a political organization’s use of a culturally resonant
symbol, competing political organizations attack the connection between that
organization’s message and the symbol. Rochon and Wolfsfeld propose a process
for the movement of policy justification symbols from interest groups and social
movements to governments. This article examines this process in the context of the
struggle among the Israeli nationalist movement, the Israeli peace movement, and
the Israeli government, identifying a typology of tactical frames applicable to research
beyond the Israeli context: denial, incorporation, and end run. Press releases
by these political competitors show a specialization of tactical frames by
social organization. Nationalists prefer to deny the validity of competing resonant
symbols. Peace activists prefer to invent or search for new symbols, in an end run.
Governments tend to absorb and redirect symbols initially used by the competing
movements to justify government actions. An analysis of the political opportunity
structures and organizational conditions that determine a political organization’s
tactics for attacking resonant frames is conducted.

publications.title: Structure of News Coverage of a Peace Process: A Test of the Indexing and Zero-Sum Hypotheses
publications.publishedAt: Harvard International Journal of Press/Politics, 8.4: 27-53 · Jan 1, 2003
publications.description:
Newspaper coverage of a peace process is crucial to the success of a peace process.
Given the critical role that newspapers play defining “others” in peace processes, it is
surprising that little research has gone into the dynamics by which newspapers portray
national “others.” Two schools of thought can apply to Western media:the indexing
hypothesis and the zero-sum hypothesis.The indexing hypothesis suggests that to
achieve balanced and unbiased coverage, newspapers will cover/cite both sides of an
issue in proportion to their relative political strength. The zero-sum hypothesis suggests
that under conditions of national stress newspapers abandon the indexing rule
and that coverage/citation of fellow nation members comes at the expense of coverage/
citation of national “others.” Logit and probit models of Israeli newspaper coverage of
the Oslo peace process from September 1995 to October 1999 show that the zero sum
hypothesis is a more accurate model. Only under favorable conditions (e.g., a
peace treaty ceremony and its political wave) does indexing operate.

publications.title: Making a Good Impression: Peace Movement Press Release Styles and Newspaper Coverage
publications.publishedAt: Harvard International Journal of Press/Politics, 7.1: 79-101 · Jan 1, 2002
publications.description:
While many studies have investigated what social and political movement actions are
covered by the mass media from a largely event-based media routine perspective and
many studies have investigated what activists want to say,few studies have looked into
the signaling process by which movements let media know when the movement has
information it wishes to express. In particular, there has been little quantitative methodological
research on the critical link that press releases provide between movements
and media.Are movement press releases more likely to be covered by the news
media when the press releases are of good quality? Using Israeli newspaper coverage
of two Israeli peace movements and press releases by the two groups, the author
tested the relevance of knowing the attributes of a press release independent of
event-based information. After controlling for time, place, and manner information
that can be derived from an event-based approach, information that can be derived
either solely from press releases or most accurately from press releases remained significant
predictors of newspaper coverage. Peace movement press releases that
(1) emphasize socially resonant themes,(2) emphasize the movement’s possession of
new factual data, (3) have short and informative titles, (4) are part of a group of
releases on the same issue or event, and (5) are written or presented by the movement’s
regular spokesperson are more likely to be reflected in newspaper media

publications.description: This study of the rearrest, reconviction, and reincarceration of prisoners tracked 272,111 former inmates for 3 years after their release in 1994. publications.title: Contacts Between Police and the Public: Findings from the 1999 National Survey
publications.description: This publication represents the annual report to the Congress as required by Section 210402 of the Violent Crime Control and Law Enforcement Act of 1994. The findings are based upon the largest self-report survey ever conducted among the U.S. resident population about contacts between the public and the police and the outcomes of those contacts. The objective of the survey was to learn more about how often and under what circumstances a traffic stop or other contact becomes problematic.

publications.title: Felony Sentences in State Courts, 1998
publications.description: In 1998 State courts convicted nearly 930,000 adults of a felony. Forty-four percent of convicted felons were sentenced to a State prison, and 24% were sentenced to a local jail (usually for a year or less). The remaining 32% were sentenced to probation. These findings come from a survey conducted every 2 years and is the Nation’s sole source of statistical information on the sentences felons receive in State courts nationwide.

publications.title: State Court Sentencing of Convicted Felons, 1996
publications.description: Prior to 1986, there were no statistics collected on the sentences convicted felons received in State courts nationwide. To close that gap, the Bureau of Justice Statistics initiated the National Judicial Reporting Program (NJRP). A pilot study was conducted in 1986. Afterwards, full-scale surveys were conducted in 1988, 1990, 1992, 1994, and 1996. The NJRP compiles information on the sentences that felons receive in State courts nationwide and on characteristics of the felons.

publications.title: Assessing the Accuracy of State Prisoner Statistics
publications.description: Included in the wide array of statistics routinely compiled and disseminated by the Bureau of Justice Statistics (BJS) are those describing persons sentenced to State prisons during the year. Prisoner characteristics are available in two different sources: BJS reports that are based on State prison records, and BJS reports that use data from State court records. This report investigates the extent to which prisoner characteristics from one source match those from the other. Results of the investigation indicate a close correspondence between court and prison records.

publications.title: Felony Sentences in State Courts, 1996
publications.description: In 1996 State courts convicted almost 998,000 adults of a felony. Thirty-eight percent of convicted felons were sentenced to a State prison, and 31% were sentenced to a local jail (usually for a year or less). The remaining 31% were sentenced to straight probation with no jail or prison time to serve. These findings come from a survey that is done every 2 years and that provides the only detailed description of the sentences felons receive in State courts nationwide.

publications.title: Photographic Literacy: Cameras in the Hands of Russian Authors
publications.description: Photography, introduced to Russia in 1839, was nothing short of a sensation. Its rapid proliferation challenged the other arts, including painting and literature, as well as the very integrity of the self. If Leo Tolstoy and Fyodor Dostoevsky greeted the camera with skepticism in the nineteenth century, numerous twentieth-century authors welcomed it with a warm embrace. As Katherine M. H. Reischl shows in Photographic Literacy, authors as varied as Leonid Andreev, Ilya Ehrenburg, and Alexander Solzhenitsyn picked up the camera and reshaped not only their writing practices but also the sphere of literacy itself.

publications.title: Controllership’s role in building an integrated ESG reporting strategy
publications.description:
The environmental, social, and governance (ESG) disclosure and reporting risk landscape has changed. Regulators globally have issued proposed and final new rules mandating ESG disclosure. For example, companies in the United States with certain significant operations in the European Union may soon be required to provide vast amounts of ESG information as mandated by the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD).
Controllership is uniquely positioned to design and implement efficient responses to the new risk calculus. And if your controllership responsibilities extend across multiple jurisdictions— domestically or internationally—you’ll likely need a view into what those continuously changing requirements are as well as processes and internal controls that are thoughtfully developed, repeatable, and sustainable. Many organizations will likely seek to introduce new (or adapt existing) technology to further that objective.

featured.title: Want to hack your brain and make the most of the holiday break? Learn something new.
featured.subtitle: Peter Hodge on LinkedIn

slides.title: Want to hack your brain and make the most of the holiday break? Learn something new.
slides.subtitle: Peter Hodge on LinkedIn
slides.description: How can you best use some down time over the holidays to come back refreshed and ready to re-engage with 2026? This was a question that I recently posed to Dr. Jesse Michel, CMPC a sports and psychology professional who helps to lead our integrated mental health program at Deloitte. Most people I ask that question to give stock answers of “spend time with my family”, “lay on the couch”, or simply “sleep”. His answer wasn’t what I expected. He said, “Learn something new”. He went on to talk about how learning something new can really help you come back from a break refreshed and ready to come out of the starting blocks like a champion. Obviously, I needed to go and research this for myself and went down a bit of a rabbit hole into the fascinating science of modern brain research. In a paper in Cell Research titled ‘To Learn Something new, do something new’ the authors Miller and Frankland used a mice experiment to test this hypothesis. In a mouse model they could see that when mice were put in a situation where they had to learn something new it actually changed the structure of their brain. Weakening existing synaptic connections in areas such as the hippocampus and prefrontal cortex. They refer to this as “cleaning the decks”. Additional research from Columbia University shows how the novelty of learning something new strengthens the brain’s theta waves. The exact same thing that happens in your brain when you go to sleep or spend time in meditation. Think about that for a moment. Learning something new is the same as other mental health restorative go to activities – mediation and sleep. But here’s the really fascinating part, learning something new can also enhance the things we already know through a process called memory reconsolidation. As best as I can deduce from overly complex science papers it works this way. When we go back to our familiar routines and expectations on Monday Jan 5th, the brain will pull up all those memories and get ready to get into the grove. However, if we have learnt something new in the interim the brain will try to fit that new information into our existing memories. It will literally rewrite those memories to enhance them with this new experience. In this way we get new insights and new creative ideas. It re-energizes our thinking and perhaps refreshes our outlook. One final benefit, which might actually be the most useful of all, and it’s to do with time. What if learning something new could actually extend your holiday break? Yes, I know you are in for this one. The idea is that by learning something new you actually alter your brains perception of time. You physically make time go slower. Think about those long summer days when you were a kid. A single day of cricket in a field that really needed to be mowed lasted forever. The reason for this is that everything was new and the brain’s perception of time is slower when it has to encode new experiences with all the information that has to be wrapped around it. I found a quote from Dr. Matt Johnson on this this: “As we age, fewer experiences are truly novel, and the brain tends to compress repetitive or familiar events, making them seem shorter in retrospect,”. There is also an amazing radiolabs podcast that discusses this phenomenon that I highly recommend listening to. The Secret to a Long Life. https://radiolab.org/podcast/secret-long-life. So, to wrap this up (holiday pun intended) it’s clear that learning something, anything, new over the break is the best way to come back feeling ready to take on 2026. You'll get all the benefits of meditation or sleeping longer. You come back to work with more clarity and creativity. And, if you learn something really cool you might eek out a couple extra days of subjective time for yourself. I’ll see you in 2026 once I’ve learnt to complete this Rubik’s cube.

slides.title: Leadership Insights from Finishing a Marathon – I Could Have Done Better
slides.subtitle: Peter Hodge on LinkedIn
slides.description: The nurse in the medical tent asked me if I knew what city I was in. That’s a strong opening question. “I started running in Chicago 2 hours ago”, I offered, “I sure hope I’m still here.” A few minutes later, with my blood pressure checked and the dizziness I had been experiencing faded, she gave me a clean bill of health. I stepped out of the tent and back into the throngs of hopeful runners. The best description of a marathon I have seen is that’s it’s a very public display of a very private battle. And that's not just about what happens on the day, but everything that leads to standing on the starting line. For me that is a deep desire to cure cystic fibrosis. I know I need to inspire people to donate to the cause so that we can buy the science that will deliver the cure. To paraphrase JFK I choose to do hard things, like run this marathon, because it is hard. And in doing so inspire others and myself. If you feel inspired a donation here would be much appreciated: https://fundraise.cff.org/chicagomarathon/areyoumad It was also an epic battle on race day too. Thankfully the extraordinary Katarina Stiles ran with me the whole race and she carried the majority of getting us through the hardest parts. I am in her debt and ever so grateful to her and her family for the continued support they show to the mission to cure cystic fibrosis. The rest of the motivation came from the nearly 2 million people lining the streets of Chicago who shouted my name and filled me with determination that at times seemed lacking. Thank you Chicago. You are a beautiful city, with beautiful people. I would have said my race performance that day didn’t win me any medals, but in fact it did. I have it sitting right on my desk as I write. It’s a physical reminder that I ran and finished a marathon. I am a marathon runner. And yet, in the days that followed the race I felt a little lost. I felt that, somehow, I had let myself and those who count on me down. I felt that I could have done better, and as a result I had somehow failed. A friend of mine who is an accomplished endurance athlete stopped me in my tracks when she told me that every race runner says the same thing – “I could have done better.” Even Conner Mantz who set a record in Chicago for the fastest ever marathon time by an American probably had the same thought roaming around in his head. I listened to an interview with him and you could hear in his words that it wasn't the record he was focused on it was the fact that he had finished 4th and hadn't made the podium. My friend's insight allowed me to reconsider how I thought about race day and it’s implications from a leadership perspective. There is an inevitable conflict built into this process. If you are the type of person who will step up to lead, to commit to the hard things, then inevitably you will also be the same person who says ”I could have done better”. This is even true when you accomplish the thing you set out to do. Simply recognizing this fact has allowed me to embrace what happened on race day. Sure I could have done better, but the fact is that I started and I finished. The 26.2 miles between those facts is merely detail. I can hold both truths in my head. I accomplished something exceptional and also I could have done better. Nothing takes away from the fact I am a marathon runner. The ten months I spent training for this marathon has been an intensely positive experience. It helped me to embrace the power of coaching and I am ever so grateful to my running coach Lisa Landrum for her expertise, positivity, and patience. She taught me the math of compound improvement that exists in consistency, and it allowed me to channel my energy into a meaningful and focused goal. It furthered my exploration of the leadership insights that exist in our everyday life. When we choose to lift our heads and embrace the stories and events around us we find those insights everywhere. It also gave me the once in a lifetime experience of racing in a major marathon. And when I say once in a lifetime I mean almost certainly, probably, most likely once in a lifetime. Did someone say London’s a great marathon to run because you know what? I am a marathon runner.

slides.title: Leadership Insights from Training for a Marathon - Actually, It's Not A Race.
slides.subtitle: Peter Hodge on LinkedIn
slides.description: On Oct 12th, 53,000 people will run in the Chicago marathon. Almost 2 million spectators will line the streets to offer cheers, encouragement, and participate in this extraordinary spectacle. I’ll be there to raise the $$, to buy the science, to cure cystic fibrosis for my daughters. If you’d be so kind as to consider a donation you can do so right here: https://fundraise.cff.org/chicagomarathon/areyoumad The marathon is a race in name, but in reality that is only true for a handful of the elite runners who will vie to cross the finish line first. As the course is one of the flattest it lends itself to fast times. Kelvin Kiptum's set a men's world record of 2:00:35 in 2023 and Ruth Chepngetich set a women's world record of 2:09:56 in 2024. For comparison the average finish time in 2024 was 4:20. I’m aiming for 5:30. So, if you can’t possibly win this thing why race? It’s because you aren’t racing against anyone else you are only racing against yourself. For first timers like me it’s the anxiety of attempting to do something that is not only hard, but is an unknown country. For those who have already proven themselves in this battle it’s a personal quest to do better, to be better. All 53,000 people who line up will have their own story as to why they are there. You know mine, but wouldn’t it be amazing to be able to peek into everyone else’s why. Like my friend Katarina Stiles who does it because she has the biggest heart and wants to cure cystic fibrosis too. Or Lou, whose two boys have a rare mutation of cystic fibrosis and he still fights for a better drug for them. For the people who run for loved ones with diseases like cancer, or heart disease, or mental illnesses. Or the people who are running this marathon because they need to prove it to themselves. Some of the best advice we can give as leaders lives right here in this message about not everything being a race. In your personal life and in the workplace it shouldn’t be a zero sum game where someone else has to lose for you to win. It doesn’t need to all progress at the same pace. The promotion will come, the big break will find you at the right time. Trying to compare yourself to someone else is a thankless road to go down. Perhaps don't listen to those influencers. What do they even know anyway? Encouraging those ‘running’ faster than you is a far better use of energy than is trying to keep up. Instead focusing that energy on who you are and what type of 'race' you want to run is guidance and leadership that we all need to hear. So, what type of 'race' do you want to run?

slides.title: Leadership Insights from Training for a Marathon – Check the half marathon box!
slides.subtitle: Peter Hodge on LinkedIn
slides.description: Last weekend I ran my first half-marathon — 13.1 miles. It wasn’t a race, no cheering crowds, no glorious finish line, just another training run. In fact, the distance was supposed to be only 12 miles, but it just seemed that putting in the effort for that extra 1.1 miles would be worth it. Darn you Garmin watch for making me beholden to your digital gamification, but that half marathon badge sure does look great on my virtual trophy shelf. It’s a fine balance between pushing yourself enough to develop those muscles and that running capacity and yet, not pushing yourself to the point of injury. Respecting rest days, focusing on your nutrition, and making sure your sleep is prioritized are all as important a part of training as is the actual running. Even before I took the first step that day, I knew that if the run went well I was going to push on to 13.1. It wasn’t just about checking off the box it was also believing in myself and in trusting the process I’ve been going through for months. In many respects a run feels a lot like a very much accelerated version of life or a work career played out in super-fast mode. There is wide-eyed optimism at the starting line and then that first mile turns out to always be the hardest. Your body and mind love homeostasis which is where it maintains a steady state. Temperature, blood sugar and fluid balance are all maintained no matter what is going on externally. It’s sort of like falling into a 9-5 where you know what to do day in and day out. It becomes routine, easy, balanced, uneventful. After that first mile is completed though it’s a wild uncertain ride. Homeostasis is thrown out the window as the body tries to react against the effects of the activity or other external factors. Temperature rises so you sweat, electrolytes can get imbalanced, muscles cramp, blisters form, joints inflame – all sorts of bad things happen as you start to chew up the miles. This is the inevitable wild ride of a long life, career, or run. It’s also the reason that change is hard. Some miles are great and you are sailing along, others you feel the weight of the world and the overwhelming desire to stop. I talked about this action crisis moment in my last blog and it’s equally as applicable in your career as it is in running. And then you are done, goal met. The effort, torment and pain all combined with hope and belief to deliver something amazing. In my book White Blaze Leadership I talk about Believe being one of my core values, a White Blaze. Like all White Blazes this faces outwards into how I believe in others, but also inwards in how I choose to believe in myself. From a leadership perspective understanding your own core values is essential to surviving a long run. Helping those around you navigate with their own White Blazes is leadership well delivered. Believing in yourself might just be the superpower Whiate Blaze that can get you through a long run or whatever change is going on in your life or work today. Right now, I choose to believe that I can run a marathon regardless of what my mind or body tries to tell me. I believe I can. In the words of the famous poet Eminem – You can do anything you set your mind to man. I also choose to believe that I can cure cystic fibrosis for my daughters. If you would like to help in that fight I’ll give you one opportunity, one moment to make a tax-free donation to the Cystic Fibrosis Foundation right here DONATE & BELIEVE. Don’t let it slip.)

slides.title: Leadership Insights from Training for a Marathon - I'm Going to Quit
slides.subtitle: Peter Hodge on LinkedIn
slides.description: “I’m going to quit.” That’s my inner voice telling me to stop. Stop believing I can run a marathon. Stop getting up early to punish myself. Stop thinking that running 6 miles on a Wednesday is normal, or that 5 miles can really be considered a so-called recovery run. Just quit. Just quit. This is a good thing that my inner voice is shouting at me. It means that I’m doing something hard. If I was a natural runner, or perhaps 30 years younger I doubt I’d be hearing that incessant voice because the task at hand would not be hard. If I had set out to run 100-mile race then I probably should have given up that goal by now. That 100-mile distance is clearly out of reach for me by October 12th which is marathon race day in Chicago. However, 26.2 miles is within reach. But, it’s also something I could fail at. It’s sort of the quantum reality of attempting something hard. The outcome is unknown until you observe it up close and personal. As much as other people give you their perspectives on training for a marathon you are the one who has to collapse this probability wave. You are the one who has to listen to that voice telling you, “it’s too hard, too much, too sore, too unlikely. Just quit.” Just quit. In Steve Magness’ excellent book ‘Do Hard Things’ he talks directly to this phenomenon of coming face to face with the prospect of failure. He tells us that psychologists call this an action crisis and defines this as “shifting from being driven to succeed to negotiating with ourselves on how to abandon the goal.” Yup that sounds about right. Have you ever been in that situation either in your personal life, or at work? When the simple act of negotiating with yourself becomes a slippery slope to the inevitable destination of 1, Quit St., Loserville. I strongly recommend Steve's book if you want to learn how to get control of doing hard things. I did some deep dive rabbit-hole research on action crisis. In a fantastic science paper titled ‘When Goal Pursuit Gets Hairy” researchers studied cortisol in subject’s hair as they experienced action crisis events across long-term (8 months) goals. The results showed that action crisis was directly connected to increases in stress, depression and ill-being. Yikes! I also spent some time thinking about why I don’t think I’ve ever experienced an action crisis when it comes to my mission to help cure cystic fibrosis. Arguably the hardest thing in my life. The answer is pretty obvious really. I don’t see failure as a potential outcome. That’s why I continue to attempt hard things as a way of raising the money that will buy the science that will cure this disease. Hey, if you are having your own action crisis right now about donating just click this link (DONATE HERE) put in your digits and consider the crisis resolved. Knowing this whole marathon action crisis stage I’m in is a normal part of dealing with something hard is really useful. I ran 10 miles last Saturday and had to spend quite a bit of my time having a conversation with my inner voice about how we could do this and how I would really appreciate it getting on board with my plan. I’ve still got some work to do to convince my inner voice of the plan. But for right now we have agreed that I am not going to quit and we agreed that the 160 beat EDM version of Eminem's Lose Yourself might just be our favorite go-to training song. I’m not quitting.

publications.title: Exploring Complementary Leader and Follower Correlates of Employee Absence
publications.publishedAt: The 29th Annual Conference of the Society for Industrial and Organizational Psychology · May 16, 2014
publications.description: This study analyzed data from 1,059 call center employees and 51 sites at a large U.S. cable/satellite provider to test linkages between absenteeism, employee attitudes, and leader traits. Results indicate that workplace environment, relevant experience, and stability of leader/follower contact matter for both leaders and followers. Low absence employees had comparatively more favorable workplace opinions, less company tenure, and more supervisor consistency. Furthermore, leaders with lower site absence had more favorable employees, less prior management experience, higher tenure, and smaller headcounts. These complementary findings suggest a need for absence strategies that address leaders and followers in tandem.

publications.title: Student Socialization in the Age of Facebook
publications.description: Most research regarding online social networks such as Facebook, MySpace, Linked-In and Friendster has looked at these networks in terms of activity within the online network, such as profile management and friending behavior. In this paper we are instead focusing on offline socializing structures around an online social network (exemplified by Facebook) and how this can facilitate in- person social life for students. Because students lead nomadic lives, they find Facebook a particularly useful tool for initiating and managing social gatherings, and as they adopt mobile technologies that can access online social networks, their ad-hoc social life is further enabled. We conclude that online social networks are a powerful tool for encouraging peripheral friendships, important in particular to students. We emphasize that the use of online social networks must be viewed from a perspective of use that involves both mobile and stationary platforms and that it is important to relate online and offline social practices.

QHUBEKA is World Bicycle Relief’s program in South Africa. Qhubeka is an Nguni word that means “to carry on” or “to move forward.”

Qhubeka is a South African non-profit that helps people move forward and progress by giving bicycles in return for work done to improve communities, the environment or academic results. Having a bicycle changes people's lives by increasing the distance they can travel, what they can carry, where they can go and how fast they can get there. Qhubeka is World Bicycle Relief’s program in South Africa.

World Bicycle Relief is a US-based non-profit organization dedicated to transforming individuals and communities through The Power of Bicycles. Since 2005, World Bicycle Relief has trained more than 1,100 field mechanics and provided more than 220,000 specially designed, locally assembled quality bicycles to disaster survivors, healthcare workers, students and entrepreneurs in the developing world.

For more information, please visit qhubeka.org and worldbicyclerelief.org

headline: Industrial/Organizational Psychologist | Behavioral Scientist | People Analytics Professional | Behavior Change, Optimal State (e.g., Flow), GenAI, and Nudge Researcher | Coach |
about:
Jared Weintraub is a Manager of People Analytics and Research at Deloitte LLP, where he focuses on defining, measuring, and improving talent experience for Deloitte professionals. His team is also responsible for designing, implementing, and analyzing rigorous measurement and evaluation plans to glean insights and provide recommendations that drive improvements for organizational initiatives affecting over 180k employees worldwide. 

Jared holds a doctorate in Applied Organizational Psychology from Hofstra University, is a certified Senior Professional in Human Resources (SPHR), and holds a master’s degree in Industrial and Organizational Psychology from the Chicago School of Professional Psychology. He is also the founder of The Flow Group, LLC., an organizational and business development firm that has worked with individuals and companies to create and maintain happy, healthy, and productive workplaces. Jared has over a decade of experience working with all levels of organizations, across various industries, ranging from rapid-growth startups to Fortune 100 companies. He has provided internal and external consulting, coaching, and managing marketing and sales teams. Dr. Weintraub has also earned certifications in Generative AI, integrated the technology into his curriculum, and provided training to students and employees on leveraging these tools effectively.

Jared is a published research-practitioner whose research primarily focuses on Flow Theory - how, when, and why individuals, teams, and organizations can get into “the Zone.” Most recently, this research has explored how we can use technology-based “nudge” solutions to drive behavioral changes that facilitate optimal states at work. He is a member of the Society of Industrial-Organizational Psychology (SIOP) and President Emeritus of the New York Metropolitan Association of Applied Psychology (METRO). Jared is an Adjunct Professor at New York University, teaching undergraduate and graduate-level I-O Psychology courses.

publications.title: Mindful multitasking: Disentangling the effect of polychronicity on work-home conflict and life satisfaction
publications.publishedAt: The Journal of Social Psychology · Oct 1, 2018
publications.description: This study seeks to disentangle the effect of polychronicity on work–home conflict, home–work conflict, and life satisfaction, by evaluating mindfulness as a moderator. We propose that mindfulness moderates the relationship between polychronicity and work–home and home–work conflict such that the relationship will be negative when mindfulness is high and positive when mindfulness is low. Additionally, we propose that mindfulness moderates the relationship between polychronicity and life satisfaction such that the relationship will be positive when mindfulness is high and negative when mindfulness is low. A total of 138 academics throughout India completed measures of polychronicity, mindfulness, life satisfaction, and work-to-home and home-to-work conflict scales. The moderation findings illustrate that higher levels of mindfulness enhance the effects of polychronicity.

projects.title: Optimization of Air Force Maintenance Scheduling
projects.associatedWith: Associated with University of Illinois at Chicago
projects.description: This project proposes an optimization approach for maintenance scheduling of Air Force aircrafts leveraging recent technologies like Internet of Things and Deep Learning. Nowadays, aircrafts are highly computerized and equipped with thousands of sensors, which changed maintenance, repair and overhaul for the Air Force. Moreover, the Air Force is striving for moderness and readiness to hold their position as a global power while reducing cost to a minimum. Therefore, aircraft and maintenance data originating from Internet of Things environments can be utilized to create Deep Learning models to forecast equipment failures. In turn, these predictions can be combined with the Air Force maintenance environment which consists of different aircraft types and fleets, maintenance types, and airbase locations, and its requirements. The proposed optimization model can be classified as a Stochastic Multi-Objective Mixed Integer Linear Programming problem with a feedback loop for the predictive machine learning model.

projects.title: Analysis of Factors and Optimization of Chicago’s Divvy Bike Rental System
projects.associatedWith: Associated with University of Illinois at Chicago
projects.description:
Bike sharing is the fastest growing type of transportation system in history. As of April 2015, there are
one thousand bike-sharing cities around the world with a total of one million bikes available for hire. 
Therefore, making bikes available when and where people need them is vital, but not trivial. The biggest
logistic challenge is moving the bikes where needed at all times. System's customers require at least one bike available when arriving at a station, and at least one parking spot available when dropping off. It is obvious that such systems run easily out of balance without proper control interaction. Thus, this project detects factors which lead to an imbalanced system, meaning factors which clear and factors which fill up stations with bikes. The analysis has been performed on real-world data of the Divvy rental system.

publications.title: Improving Predictive Process Monitoring Through Reachability Graph-Based Masking of Neural Networks
publications.publishedAt: IEEE Transactions on Computational Social Systems · Nov 18, 2022
publications.description: Predicting the next event during process runtime is an objective of interest in predictive process monitoring (PPM). Decay replay mining is one of few deep learning-based next event prediction approaches that are built upon process model notations. However, this algorithm does not fully intertwine its neural network with the available process knowledge contained in the process model. This work, which is an extended version of an earlier conference publication, investigates the reachability graphs of underlying Petri net process models for masking the neural network of decay replay mining to ultimately increase the quality of next event predictions. A more comprehensive set of experiments is performed to provide robust statistical evidence of the usefulness of the approach and relativizes earlier made claims and hypotheses. In addition, the decay replay mining approach is applied with the suggested reachability graph-based masking extension to a healthcare use case of sepsis patients facilitating decision-making for healthcare practitioners. The obtained results further underscore the validity of the masking of neural networks using knowledge contained in the reachability graph of a Petri net process model.

publications.title: On the Performance Analysis of the Adversarial System Variant Approximation Method to Quantify Process Model Generalization
publications.publishedAt: ICPM 2021: Process Mining Workshops. Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing. · Mar 24, 2022
publications.description: Process mining algorithms discover a process model from an event log. The resulting process model is supposed to describe all possible event sequences of the underlying system. Generalization is a process model quality dimension of interest. A generalization metric should quantify the extent to which a process model represents the observed event sequences contained in the event log and the unobserved event sequences of the system. Most of the available metrics in the literature cannot properly quantify the generalization of a process model. A recently published method called Adversarial System Variant Approximation leverages Generative Adversarial Networks to approximate the underlying event sequence distribution of a system from an event log. While this method demonstrated performance gains over existing methods in measuring the generalization of process models, its experimental evaluations have been performed under ideal conditions. This paper experimentally investigates the performance of Adversarial System Variant Approximation under non-ideal conditions such as biased and limited event logs. Moreover, experiments are performed to investigate the originally proposed sampling hyperparameter value of the method on its performance to measure the generalization. The results confirm the need to raise awareness about the working conditions of the Adversarial System Variant Approximation method. The outcomes of this paper also serve to initiate future research directions.

publications.title: Masking Neural Networks Using Reachability Graphs to Predict Process Events
publications.publishedAt: 2021 International Conference on Cyber-Physical Social Intelligence (ICCSI) · Mar 23, 2022
publications.description: Decay Replay Mining is a deep learning method that utilizes process model notations to predict the next event. However, this method does not intertwine the neural network with the structure of the process model to its full extent. This paper proposes an approach to further interlock the process model of Decay Replay Mining with its neural network for next event prediction. The approach uses a masking layer which is initialized based on the reachability graph of the process model. Additionally, modifications to the neural network architecture are proposed to increase the predictive performance. Experimental results demonstrate the value of the approach and underscore the importance of discovering precise and generalized process models.

publications.title: Predicting clinical outcomes among hospitalized COVID-19 patients using both local and published models
publications.publishedAt: BMC Medical Informatics and Decision Making · Jul 23, 2021
publications.description:
Background
Many models are published which predict outcomes in hospitalized COVID-19 patients. The generalizability of many is unknown. We evaluated the performance of selected models from the literature and our own models to predict outcomes in patients at our institution.

Methods
We searched the literature for models predicting outcomes in inpatients with COVID-19. We produced models of mortality or criticality (mortality or ICU admission) in a development cohort. We tested external models which provided sufficient information and our models using a test cohort of our most recent patients. The performance of models was compared using the area under the receiver operator curve (AUC).

Results
Our literature review yielded 41 papers. Of those, 8 were found to have sufficient documentation and concordance with features available in our cohort to implement in our test cohort. All models were from Chinese patients. One model predicted criticality and seven mortality. Tested against the test cohort, internal models had an AUC of 0.84 (0.74–0.94) for mortality and 0.83 (0.76–0.90) for criticality. The best external model had an AUC of 0.89 (0.82–0.96) using three variables, another an AUC of 0.84 (0.78–0.91) using ten variables. AUC’s ranged from 0.68 to 0.89. On average, models tested were unable to produce predictions in 27% of patients due to missing lab data.

Conclusion
Despite differences in pandemic timeline, race, and socio-cultural healthcare context some models derived in China performed well. For healthcare organizations considering implementation of an external model, concordance between the features used in the model and features available in their own patients may be important. Analysis of both local and external models should be done to help decide on what prediction method is used to provide clinical decision support to clinicians treating COVID-19 patients as well as what lab tests should be included in order sets.

publications.title: Improving the In-Hospital Mortality Prediction of Diabetes ICU Patients Using a Process Mining/Deep Learning Architecture
publications.publishedAt: IEEE Journal of Biomedical and Health Informatics · Jun 27, 2021
publications.description: Diabetes intensive care unit (ICU) patients are at increased risk of complications leading to in-hospital mortality. Assessing the likelihood of death is a challenging and time consuming task due to a large number of influencing factors. Healthcare providers are interested in the detection of ICU patients at higher risk, such that risk factors can possibly be mitigated. While such severity scoring methods exist, they are commonly based on a snapshot of the health conditions of a patient during the ICU stay and do not specifically consider a patient's prior medical history. In this paper, a process mining/deep learning architecture is proposed to improve established severity scoring methods by incorporating the medical history of diabetes patients. First, health records of past hospital encounters are converted to event logs suitable for process mining. The event logs are then used to discover a process model that describes the past hospital encounters of patients. An adaptation of Decay Replay Mining is proposed to combine medical and demographic information with established severity scores to predict the in hospital mortality of diabetes ICU patients. Significant performance improvements are demonstrated compared to established risk severity scoring methods and machine learning approaches using the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care III dataset.

publications.title: Adversarial System Variant Approximation to Quantify Process Model Generalization
publications.description: In process mining, process models are extracted from event logs using process discovery algorithms and are commonly assessed using multiple quality metrics. While the metrics that measure the relationship of an extracted process model to its event log are well-studied, quantifying the level by which a process model can describe the unobserved behavior of its underlying system falls short in the literature. In this paper, a novel deep learning-based methodology called Adversarial System Variant Approximation (AVATAR) is proposed to overcome this issue. Sequence Generative Adversarial Networks are trained on the variants contained in an event log with the intention to approximate the underlying variant distribution of the system behavior. Unobserved realistic variants are sampled either directly from the Sequence Generative Adversarial Network or by leveraging the Metropolis-Hastings algorithm. The degree by which a process model relates to its underlying unknown system behavior is then quantified based on the realistic observed and estimated unobserved variants using established process model quality metrics. Significant performance improvements in revealing realistic unobserved variants are demonstrated in a controlled experiment on 15 ground truth systems. Additionally, the proposed methodology is experimentally tested and evaluated to quantify the generalization of 60 discovered process models with respect to their systems.

publications.title: Decay Replay Mining to Predict Next Process Events
publications.description: In complex processes, various events can happen in different sequences. The prediction of the next event given an a-priori process state is of importance in such processes. Recent methods have proposed deep learning techniques such as recurrent neural networks, developed on raw event logs, to predict the next event from a process state. However, such deep learning models by themselves lack a clear representation of the process states. At the same time, recent methods have neglected the time feature of event instances. In this paper, we take advantage of Petri nets as a powerful tool in modeling complex process behaviors considering time as an elemental variable. We propose an approach which starts from a Petri net process model constructed by a process mining algorithm. We enhance the Petri net model with time decay functions to create continuous process state samples. Finally, we use these samples in combination with discrete token movement counters and Petri net markings to train a deep learning model that predicts the next event. We demonstrate significant performance improvements and outperform the state-of-the-art methods on nine real-world benchmark event logs.

publications.title: Behavioral Petri Net Mining and Automated Analysis for Human-Computer Interaction Recommendations in Multi-Application Environments
publications.publishedAt: Proceedings of the ACM on Human-Computer Interaction - EICS · Jun 1, 2019
publications.description: Process Mining is a famous technique which is frequently applied to Software Development Processes, while being neglected in Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) recommendation applications. Organizations usually train employees to interact with required IT systems. Often, employees, or users in general, develop their own strategies for solving repetitive tasks and processes. However, organizations find it hard to detect whether employees interact efficiently with IT systems or not. Hence, we have developed a method which detects inefficient behavior assuming that at least one optimal HCI strategy is known. This method provides recommendations to gradually adapt users' behavior towards the optimal way of interaction considering satisfaction of users. Based on users' behavior logs tracked by a Java application suitable for multi-application and multi-instance environments, we demonstrate the applicability for a specific task in a common Windows environment utilizing realistic simulated behaviors of users.

publications.title: Process Mining of Programmable Logic Controllers: Input/Output Event Logs
publications.publishedAt: 2019 IEEE 15th International Conference on Automation Science and Engineering (CASE), Vancouver, BC, Canada · Mar 22, 2019
publications.description: This paper presents an approach to model an unknown Ladder Logic based Programmable Logic Controller (PLC) program consisting of Boolean logic and counters using Process Mining techniques. First, we tap the inputs and outputs of a PLC to create a data flow log. Second, we propose a method to translate the obtained data flow log to an event log suitable for Process Mining. In a third step, we propose a hybrid Petri net (PN) and neural network approach to approximate the logic of the actual underlying PLC program. We demonstrate the applicability of our proposed approach on a case study with three simulated scenarios.

projects.title: Live Well Vive Bien
projects.description:
Live Well Vive Bien is a collaborative project of Equidad ATX. Live Well Vive Bien is not intended to replace brick and mortar facilities but a significant bridge until that happens. Equidad ATX, a tax-exempt charitable organization, is a catalyst for holistic, equitable, sustainable, and transformative neighborhood revitalization and disruption of the cycle of generational poverty in Austin’s “Eastern Crescent.” 

The initial concept for Live Well/Vive Bien was to create a holistic mobile ecosystem servicing the communities of Colony Park, Creedmore, and Del Valle that aimed to address social needs affecting overall health. The idea revolves around one bus donated by CapMetro that will be retrofitted to become a mobile grocery store.  The plan was that the bus would drive to the designated neighborhoods on scheduled days and provide residents with healthy food at low cost.  However, the COVID-19 pandemic has disrupted this initial plan: it is now unsafe for residents to enter the bus.

Our current assets are one bus, designated pilot areas and numerous community partnerships that Equidad ATX/Live Well has previously established.Additionally, we desire to co-design concepts with the residents of our target communities and the community partners.

Our challenge now is to reframe this initial concept into a design that is both safe during the COVID-19 pandemic and sustainable beyond it. An additional and important goal for this service is to create a holistic customer experience exemplifying dignity and respect for all. We have summarized our design challenge in the following “How Might We” statement: how might we best utilize our available assets to design a sustainable and holistic experience within our target communities that aims to address food insecurity in a dignified and COVID-safe manner?

about:
Hi, there! I am a strategy and operations consultant with more than 10 years of experience leading cross-functional teams in government, tech, non-profit, and research environments.

In my current role, I support executives in the development of product and service strategies and the delivery of large-scale transformations (e.g. digital, cultural, strategic, etc.). To this end, I have lead discovery and design for public interest technologies as a scrum master; implemented federal IT modernizations in change-resistant environments; developed public-facing solutions to increase transparency in policy implementation; and consulted on environmental sustainability for leaders in Europe's transportation and hospitality industry.  

Prior to my current role, I spent 5 years managing social services programs in Chicago, Illinois. Herein I worked to increase access to higher education, affordable housing, healthcare, and financial supports for low-income families. I drove initiatives that connected more than 600 households with vital social services and raised over $4 million for community development initiatives. 

My specialties as an culture & belonging consultant include inclusion strategy and curriculum development. To this end, I have conducted culture audits (e.g. at the process, program, and organization level) and facilitated the development of cultural transformation plans. I have delivered  workshops to more than 400 working professionals and youth -- including material on inclusive leadership, racial equity in urban development, effective mentorship, culturally competent program evaluation, and LGBTQIA inclusivity in the workplace.

I am a graduate of Carnegie Mellon University's quantitatively rigorous Master of Science, Public Policy & Management program, where I specialized in public policy analysis and applied statistics (e.g. causal inference, predictive modelling, survey design). My time as a scholar abroad at the Bocconi SDA School of Management also provided me with a practical foundation in behavioral and decision science, organizational strategy and design, business process modelling, and change management.

When I am not buried under logic models, I am a poet, songwriter, and avid home cook with a passion for community-based arts.

experience.description:
Since 1986, East Village Youth Program has been advancing education equity through college access and youth development services for low income families on Chicago's Northwest Side. As one of EVYP's Program Managers, I lead the development, implementation, and evaluation of education initiatives that reach 5th - 10th grade students. These initiatives include:

- The East Village Youth Program Leadership Institute (founder), where up to 30 High School Freshman and Sophomores tackle issues of justice and equity through intensive weekly sessions. Participants receive leadership training, explore issues in their communities, gain community organizing skills (e.g. stakeholder analysis, project management, proposal writing, communications, etc.), and pursue service learning projects. 

- After School Tutoring, which connects up to 60 students (5th grade - 10th grade) with committed volunteers for homework help and academic enrichment activities on a weekly basis. Since joining EVYP, I've introduced creative exercises to build community between tutors and students, as well as implemented surveys to assist in structuring session time and capture qualitative data on student experience.  

- Cultural Empowerment and Enrichment, where we activate EVYP's commitment to nurturing the cultural wealth of our community by organizing affirming events, field trips, and other activities. This initiative balances a need for formal college access services such as career panels and college visits with the development of cultural capital through community service outings, talks with local artists, film screenings, and more. 

- College Bound: Career Exploration, a partnership with After School Matters that introduces youth to pathways for pursuing careers that require a college degree. During interactive workshops and field trips, youth explore different colleges and careers, enhance their writing skills, learn how to create a resume, write a cover letter, interview strategies, etc.

Gozamos is an independent online magazine focused on Latino arts + activism. Through community partnerships, we put our words into action to inspire, educate and entertain. Under Gozamos, I've pitched and published numerous articles related to the Latino experience in Chicago, including Arts & Culture, Education, and Politics. Moreover, I've worked as an organizer within our team to create impactful cultural events which serve as a creative meeting point for marginalized populations.

During my two years at LUCHA, I managed a grant calendar with over 100 leads for a medium-sized 501c(3) focusing on affordable housing, community development, and supportive services for Chicago's low-to-moderate residents of color. Within my first year, I crafted proposals to secure over $500,000 in new revenue to while maintaining a funding stream of over $1,000,000; significant relationships to this end included the U.S. Department of Justice, the Illinois Housing Development Authority, and Enterprise Community Partners.

I was able to accomplish this by developing innovative program models that leveraged extensive research in social policy fields (e.g. violence against women, LGBTQ, fair housing, financial empowerment, public health etc.), data analysis, and efficient utilization of client relationship management systems. I established key frameworks for approaching organizational partnerships, as well, by adopting Collective Impact Theory; formalized a communications and accountability process for the development team; and pushed LUCHA to pursue programs to address the marginalization of LGBTQ populations in the housing market.

Please see the links below for programs which were the focus of my research, development, and fundraising work at LUCHA and continue to thrive under their awesome leadership!

As outreach coordinator of the PRCC's Esperanza project, I created and implemented a community outreach plan meant to link over 100 residents of Chicago’s west side with mental health services through case management and service coordination. To this end, I conducted on-the-streets interviews, social media campaigns, and established partnerships with local hospitals, shelters, churches, high schools, and advocacy groups to identify program-eligible residents and combat the stigmatization of mental illness.

headline: Government and Public Sector Organizational Change | Educator | 20 Years of Public Sector Experience
about:
I am a driven and innovative professional with over 15 years of experience in applying organizational change management strategies in the public sector. My goal is to assist mid- to high-level executives who want to improve their organizational culture and change initiatives based on research, cultural analysis, and practical implementation. 

I have more than 17 years of phenomenological experience in the field of law enforcement ranging from a front-line officer, investigator, field commander, and executive administrator. One of my largest accomplishments was breaking through stigmas of 20-plus-year police department veterans and engaging fresh, new officers by transitioning our paper-based reporting system database to digital. This was a multi-year process that required support and communication across multiple teams. 

Additionally, I have demonstrated a progressive nature with academic teaching positions, curriculum development public speaking, and peer-reviewed research initiatives. 

I take pride in my professional growth, which is one of the reasons I obtained my Ph.D.in Organizational Leadership and continue to inspire both young and executive-level minds at Northwestern University and The Peele Group. 

My volunteer work in the community spans from the Illinois Special Olympics to PAV YMCA Board of Directors, Chicago Council of Global Affairs to Thrive Leadership Chicago. Furthermore, I am proud to be an art collector and perennial endurance sport participant. 

If you would like to connect or know more about my professional story, please send me an InMail message or email me at jfboracay@gmail.com.

publications.title: Police Leadership and the Importance of Organizational Alignment
publications.publishedAt: Command Magazine (Illinois Chiefs of Police) · Feb 1, 2015
publications.description:
As police leaders continue to run organizations that encounter more complex situations, such as growing crime rates, employee disenchantment, and financial constraints, they need models, best practices, and strategies in order to successfully deal with these particular issues.  Research suggests that one of the keys to stellar organizational performance in the private sector is organizational alignment while another is strong leadership that serves a purpose.  

A recurring theme among law enforcement professionals is that those who were unhappy with their workplace operated under a structure that had very inconsistent leadership, while those who were happy with their job environment worked for leaders who shared similar leadership styles.  This article discusses whether the alignment of leadership styles in law enforcement agencies affects the engagement of their employees and thus the productivity of their organizations.

about:
Shaun is a Strategy Principal at Throughline, bringing visual language (with her very talented colleagues) to her clients’ most complex strategies and processes. She is a former CPA and partner (now retired) at Deloitte LLP on assignment to DTTL, Deloitte’s Global Firm. She was part of the Global Audit Innovation Leadership team and supported Global Audit Strategy initiatives. 

Prior to her global leadership role, she was president of the U.S. Deloitte Foundation, a nonprofit organization that supports educational programming that is shaping the talent of the future. Shaun helped the Foundation to expand its support of existing academic programs and to develop new programs to address challenges facing the business.

A catalyst for women’s advancement, Shaun has spoken at many conferences on issues facing women in the workplace.  She was Deloitte’s National Director for the Retention and Advancement of Women. 

Shaun Previously was a Partner (now retired) and the KPMG Audit Innovation Leader, steering the audit practice’s journey to transform the audit culture and professional mindset so that KPMG is positioned to deliver high quality and relevant audits. In her role, she  implemented new governance models, programs and technologies to advance the audit practice’s people, processes and technologies. 

She established the Audit Innovation Leaders Network, a collaborative group of partners across the firm dedicated to encouraging new ways of thinking and educating the practice on how the technology transformation will impact the audit. In addition, she’s started a series of planning labs for auditors to apply innovative design thinking and collective techniques to their engagements and visioning sessions to raise awareness about an innovative culture and marketplace trends. Shaun served on the judging panel of the firm’s first ever Audit Innovation Challenge and was instrumental in making this “Shark Tank” type challenge a reality at KPMG. 

She served on KPMG’s Women’s Advisory Board, dedicated to creating a compelling work environment and enhancing career opportunities for women.

headline: Senior Consultant, Deloitte Consulting LLP ■ Chicago Booth MBA ■ PMP ■ Innovating Enterprise Solutions, Streamlining Industry Processes, Building Client Relationships
about:
I’m passionate about working with my team on a shared vision to deliver innovative solutions. I am data-driven from my experience, and I am engaged by collaborating on creative options to present to my clients.

My colleagues and I must pay attention to details, although I also like to integrate and think about the big picture. 

I’m fascinated by the intersection of business strategy and technology, and I’m currently working on a Booth MBA. The larger questions surrounding innovation and market opportunities intrigue me. 

I bring 15+ years of engineering management and PMP experience to my role in Deloitte Consulting. My industry expertise is in aerospace & defense, industrial manufacturing, program management, digital PLM and supply chain solutions.

Ultimately, I hope my work will provide enduring value for my clients as well as society as a whole. I think about the advancements in communication, transportation, and technology over the last 100 years and wonder what the world will look like in the 2100s. Even if my personal contributions are just one piece in the puzzle, I execute my work to be part of the path forward.

When I’m not working, you’ll usually find me spending time with my wife, two daughters, and two dogs. Some of my favorite activities are hiking, lifting weights, grilling, following sports, and attending Broadway shows.

headline: Strategy Leader, Experience & Human-centred place design, ‘Expedition Leader’ | Planet-Centricity | Optimist + Futurist | Globe wanderer & seeker of light.
about:
Experienced advisor, leader and designer with a focus on strategy and transformation in both public and private sectors. Proven history of visioning & shaping Experience Strategies and delivering impact. Passionate about transforming our complex systems, cities, environments, services and experiences to be more human and sustainable.  Energised by leading teams and stakeholders through the process of understanding how things work, and how they could work. 

I'm passionate about designing our preferred future and the transitions that will take us there.  It's about having a way to manage massive change and having fun creatively shaping our future. 

To create scaled impact, I have specialised in the co-design of transitions and programs that improve how we work, live, and interact in our shared spaces or services. This might be a public service, a workplace, a campus, an airport, an innovation district, a smart city, or the organisations and services that call them home.  This is more than service design - its systems-led design that seeks to bring together people, place, planet and platforms into a single story.  

I'm also an accomplished service designer and experience strategist. Over many years I've built digital products, government policies, organisational transformations and innovation programs. 

Put simply, I lead programs and teams to reimagine and redesign places, systems and organisations - as well their parts - to be more valuable, vibrant and sustainable. 

I provide clarity of action for decision-makers and pioneering organisations who are making choices about their future. 

I have more than 18 years experience in the application of holistic consulting and creative methods. Exploring the application of foresight/futures exploration, co-design, anthropology, design thinking, systems thinking, placemaking and behavioural sciences along with pragmatic approaches such as business design, Agile, Lean Start-Up, organisational design and program delivery.

publications.title: 13 Mistakes that Organisations Make When Becoming Customer Centric
publications.description:
Customer-centric behaviour promises everything and demands more. It offers great rewards and guarantees disruption to business as usual.

This book seeks to navigate the challenges for those who are considering or in the process of implementing customer-centric initiatives. It highlights 13 mistakes that can prove disastrous to customer-centric thinking.

publications.title: The Lens - An engineered space for strategy and program transformation
publications.description: Many organisations are facing increasingly complex environments both internally and externally. Key to success in this environment is the eﬀective use of the insight, wisdom and energy that is available to us. This is enabled through creating a space for people to draw a breath and think about aspects of the problems in a way that is bigger than the day-to-day decision-making. The space breaks cultural norms in how decisions are made to open new insights and areas of opportunity. This is achieved by creating an environment where dialogue is engineered so people can act and think in new ways. The Lens can take multiple forms to eﬀectively cultivate awareness, support transformation and managing complexity. The challenge is to bring humanity back to organisations, to give them permission to have conversations, to collaborate, to surprise and to innovate.

projects.title: Search of Spatio-temporal Resources
projects.description:
The aim of these simulations is to compare and contrast different algorithms, with different levels of information access to find parking spots in real time. The setup is done for the city of San Francisco, CA. We use the data released by the parking authorities, ranging over a month, given with timestamps accurate to second granularity.

We simulated the experiments on a web-based interface, running on Tomcat 8 server and SQL Server 2012 used as the database server. The simulations assume the given time-stamped availability data as the real-time data, with no information to the future data.

So we had to perform the following tasks
1. Task 1: To evaluate different algorithms to find a parking spot for the user with high level of information on a real time dataset, like parking block, parking availability, date and time, user destination and start location.
2. Task 2: To evaluate different algorithms to find a parking spot for a user with limited level of information, like parking block, start location, destination location and time, and the dataset is probabilistic rather than real time.
3. Task 3: To find a parking spot for a user in an uninformed search with only information of user destination, starting location and parking block.

headline: Senior Solution Specialist, Communications Hub at Deloitte
about:
As both an editor and writer, I'm driven, detail-oriented, and conscientious. I always aim to do the best possible work, not only for myself but for the company I work at, and I strive to make my work have a greater impact on the population at large.

I have multiple years' experience in ERP implementation, specifically the Workday Financials system, in both corporate and educational environments.

experience.position: Employer Brand and Internal Communications Specialist

experience.description:
I was the Sr. Specialist in the Internal Communications department at the Sprouts Farmers Market Support Office. Within the Internal Communications team at Sprouts, I work on crafting and disseminating communications in various media (emails, PowerPoint, videos, etc.) for the larger internal audience at Sprouts, which comprises of tens of thousands of store team members across 22 states. 

Throughout my tenure at Sprouts, I've shepherded internal newsletters for store and corporate team members. This entails working with stakeholders on timely stories, which are intended to be engaging, insightful, and educational. Initially, these newsletters were created for both print and digital use; due to the COVID-19 pandemic, these newsletters have become digital-only messaging for team members. 

I serve as the lead on all human resource-related communications, as well as sustainability communications; this includes a monthly human resources newsletter, as well as all materials related to the annual benefits enrollment initiative. Within the benefits initiative, I serve as communications lead to make sure that all materials were created within design and subject specifications, and that all team members across the country were given materials necessary to their specific benefits requirements.

I also review ad hoc and regularly planned email communications to be distributed to all team members with email accounts; review and offer suggestions on any internal presentations; and work to make sure all internal communications have a shared, consistent voice.

I was the Communications Lead on the Organizational Change Management team for the Workday implementation project. This ERP implementation was a university-wide change, introducing the cloud-based Workday Financials software to the university community. 

Within this project, I worked on crafting and disseminating communications in various media (emails, PowerPoint, videos, etc.) to help ready the user base for this impending change. I helped build up and maintain a new section of the ASU CFO website to house all Workday content. 

Throughout the project, I worked with functional area leads to pinpoint appropriate communication needs and audiences. I supervised a new communications specialist, who I interviewed, hired, and on-boarded, to help meet the Workday Project's communications needs.

I worked in the Financial Services department at Arizona State University as a Communications Specialist, managing change and communications for the implementation of the My ASU TRIP travel system, a modern cloud-based system with SAP-Concur software. In this project, I communicated system changes to more than 10,000 faculty, staff and student workers. I created and edited work instructions, job aids, videos, and maintained templates for each of those communication types.

In this position, I also helped on-board two training specialists, with whom I created and produced an update to existing financial training documentation. I also worked with department leads and a technical team on migration of past site content to a new, streamlined website via Drupal content management.

For nearly six years, I worked in the Instructional Design & Development Department at University of Phoenix. First, I was classified as an editor, but in 2010, I was promoted to senior status, thanks in part to my mentoring my colleagues and becoming more involved in high-level projects that affected worldwide students and faculty.  
 
As part of my day-to-day duties, I edited and, when necessary, helped reshape and rewrite various materials for courses and projects in the University of Phoenix educational system. In the process of working on these materials, I utilized my knowledge of various stylistic formats, from MLA to APA to the Chicago Manual of Style. I was responsible for meeting manager- and stakeholder-decreed deadlines, often dealing with multiple projects on any given day, week, or month. In my tenure at University of Phoenix, I created and helped shape templates upon which future materials were built and developed.
